REGISTRY OF CHARITABLE TRUSTS — REGISTRATION AND ANNUAL REPORTING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Community Foundation

REGISTRY OF CHARITABLE TRUSTS INFORMATION SHEET DECLARATION
This information sheet, prepared by Pat Morgan in connection with Acme Community Foundation, describes California's Registry of Charitable Trusts registration and annual reporting requirements administered by the Attorney General under the Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, Government Code sections 12580 through 12599.10. It states generally applicable California law on a general informational basis only. It does not evaluate whether Acme Community Foundation is required to register or report under this article, does not determine Acme Community Foundation's current registration, reporting, or good-standing status with the Attorney General's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers, and does not determine Acme Community Foundation's federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate determination made by the Internal Revenue Service.

WHO MUST REGISTER: ENTITIES HOLDING PROPERTY FOR CHARITABLE PURPOSES
California's Registry of Charitable Trusts, administered by the Attorney General under the Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, applies broadly to entities that hold or solicit property for charitable purposes, not only to incorporated nonprofits. By statute, the article governing the Registry "applies to all charitable corporations, unincorporated associations, trustees, and other legal entities holding property for charitable purposes, commercial fundraisers for charitable purposes, fundraising counsel for charitable purposes, commercial coventurers, charitable fundraising platforms, and platform charities over which the state or the Attorney General has enforcement or supervisory powers." A separate statutory definition extends "trustee" status — and with it registration coverage — beyond formal trust arrangements: it reaches (among others) “any individual, group of individuals, corporation, unincorporated association, or other legal entity holding property in trust pursuant to any charitable trust,” “any corporation or unincorporated association which has accepted property to be used for a particular charitable purpose as distinguished from the general purposes of the corporation or unincorporated association,” and “a corporation or unincorporated association formed for the administration of a charitable trust, pursuant to the directions of the settlor or at the instance of the trustee." Coverage is not universal, however: a separate statute exempts several categories outright from the article's filing, registration, and reporting provisions, stating that those provisions "do not apply to the United States, any state, territory, or possession of the United States, the District of Columbia, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or to any of their agencies or governmental subdivisions, to any religious corporation sole or other religious corporation or organization that holds property for religious purposes," and separately exempting "a charitable corporation or unincorporated association organized and operated primarily as a religious organization, educational institution, hospital, or a health care service plan licensed pursuant to Section 1349 of the Health and Safety Code."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This article applies to all charitable corporations, unincorporated associations, trustees, and other legal entities holding property for charitable purposes, commercial fundraisers for charitable purposes, fundraising counsel for charitable purposes, commercial coventurers, charitable fundraising platforms, and platform charities over which the state or the Attorney General has enforcement or supervisory powers."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12581, Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, the article's scope of application (current text, operative January 1, 2023) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12581.)
  "“Trustee” means (a) any individual, group of individuals, corporation, unincorporated association, or other legal entity holding property in trust pursuant to any charitable trust, (b) any corporation or unincorporated association which has accepted property to be used for a particular charitable purpose as distinguished from the general purposes of the corporation or unincorporated association, and (c) a corporation or unincorporated association formed for the administration of a charitable trust, pursuant to the directions of the settlor or at the instance of the trustee."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12582, Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, the statutory definition of “trustee” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12582.)
  "The filing, registration, and reporting provisions of this article do not apply to the United States, any state, territory, or possession of the United States, the District of Columbia, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or to any of their agencies or governmental subdivisions, to any religious corporation sole or other religious corporation or organization that holds property for religious purposes"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12583, Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, exemption for government entities and religious corporations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12583.)
  "or to a charitable corporation or unincorporated association organized and operated primarily as a religious organization, educational institution, hospital, or a health care service plan licensed pursuant to Section 1349 of the Health and Safety Code."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12583, Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, exemption for organizations operated primarily as a religious organization, educational institution, hospital, or licensed health care service plan (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12583.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on three independently enacted sections of the same statutory article — Cal. Gov. Code §§ 12581, 12582, and 12583 — treated as three independent sources. The two citations below drawn from § 12583 are two non-adjacent excerpts of that same single section (separated by unquoted statutory text addressing cemetery corporations and certain campaign-finance committees) and are treated together as one source, not as two independent corroborating ones. Section 12581's current text was added by a 2021 amendment (Stats. 2021, Ch. 616 (AB 488)), effective January 1, 2022 and operative January 1, 2023, which repealed and replaced an earlier version of the section; the text quoted here is the current, operative text, and it is broader than older descriptions of this article might suggest — it now expressly reaches "charitable fundraising platforms" and "platform charities," categories the pre-2023 statute did not name. This clause does not cover the further, narrower exemption for "corporate trustees which are subject to the jurisdiction of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions... or to the Comptroller of the Currency," which appears in a different section (Cal. Gov. Code § 12586(a)) addressed in this document's annual-reporting clause rather than here. The religious-corporation exemption quoted here is the same statutory text already cited, from a different angle (the narrower, separate limit on the Attorney General's regulatory powers over religious corporations specifically), in this project's Nonprofit Religious Corporation document; citing it again here, in the context of who must register with the Registry generally, states an independent point and is not a repetition of that document's distinct one. This clause states which categories of entity the statute names as covered or exempt; it does not evaluate whether any specific organization falls into a covered or exempt category, and it does not address federal 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status, which is a separate federal question this clause does not reach.

INITIAL REGISTRATION AND ITS 30-DAY DEADLINE
Registration with the Attorney General's Registry of Charitable Trusts is a distinct, ongoing filing obligation separate from formation with the California Secretary of State, and by statute it is triggered by receipt of property, not by the act of incorporating. The statute provides that "every charitable corporation, unincorporated association, and trustee subject to this article shall file with the Attorney General an initial registration form, under oath, setting forth information and attaching documents prescribed in accordance with rules and regulations of the Attorney General, within 30 days after the corporation, unincorporated association, or trustee initially receives property. A trustee is not required to register as long as the charitable interest in a trust is a future interest, but shall do so within 30 days after any charitable interest in a trust becomes a present interest." The Attorney General's own public guidance on this filing states the same 30-day rule in plain terms: "Charitable organizations are required to register with the Registry of Charities and Fundraisers within 30 days of the initial receipt of assets." To administer this and related filings, the Attorney General is separately directed by statute to "establish and maintain a register of charitable corporations, unincorporated associations, and trustees subject to this article and of the particular trust or other relationship under which they hold property for charitable purposes."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Every charitable corporation, unincorporated association, and trustee subject to this article shall file with the Attorney General an initial registration form, under oath, setting forth information and attaching documents prescribed in accordance with rules and regulations of the Attorney General, within 30 days after the corporation, unincorporated association, or trustee initially receives property. A trustee is not required to register as long as the charitable interest in a trust is a future interest, but shall do so within 30 days after any charitable interest in a trust becomes a present interest."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12585(a), Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, the initial registration filing requirement and its 30-day deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12585.)
  "The Attorney General shall establish and maintain a register of charitable corporations, unincorporated associations, and trustees subject to this article and of the particular trust or other relationship under which they hold property for charitable purposes"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12584, Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, the Attorney General's duty to maintain the register (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12584.)
  "Charitable organizations are required to register with the Registry of Charities and Fundraisers within 30 days of the initial receipt of assets."
  — California Attorney General, Registry of Charities and Fundraisers, “Initial Registration” page (state agency guidance page), California DOJ, Office of the Attorney General, Charities — Initial Registration (https://oag.ca.gov/charities/initial-reg)
  Known gap: Cal. Gov. Code § 12585 and Cal. Gov. Code § 12584 are independently enacted sections of the same statutory article and are treated as two independent sources; the Attorney General's initial-registration webpage is cited separately as a third, non-statutory source that restates the same 30-day rule in the agency's own words — it corroborates, but is not itself, the statutory text, and this document independently fetched and verified its wording (retrieved twice with different User-Agent strings, byte-identical after whitespace normalization). This clause states only the timing trigger and its statutory deadline; it does not describe the contents required on the initial registration form itself (the statute delegates that content to Attorney General regulations, which this clause does not independently fetch or quote), and it does not address what counts, in any specific factual situation, as the corporation, association, or trustee having "initially received property." It also does not address the separate registration and bonding obligations this same article imposes on commercial fundraisers, fundraising counsel, commercial coventurers, charitable fundraising platforms, and platform charities, which are governed by other provisions of the article not covered by this clause.

ANNUAL REPORTING: FORM RRF-1 AND FINANCIAL DISCLOSURES
Once registered, a charitable corporation, unincorporated association, or trustee subject to the Registry is subject to a recurring, not merely one-time, reporting duty. The statute requires that, with certain exceptions, "every charitable corporation, unincorporated association, and trustee subject to this article shall, in addition to filing copies of the instruments previously required, file with the Attorney General periodic written reports, under oath, setting forth information as to the nature of the assets held for charitable purposes and the administration thereof by the corporation, unincorporated association, or trustee, in accordance with rules and regulations of the Attorney General." The statute itself fixes the deadline for the first such report: "The first periodic written report, unless the filing thereof is suspended as herein provided, shall be filed not later than four months and 15 days following the close of the first calendar or fiscal year in which property is initially received" — the same four-months-and-15-days period that governs each subsequent annual report. The Attorney General's Registry implements this statutory duty through a specific numbered form: its own guidance states that "the Form RRF-1 is a form to renew an existing registration to report on the charity's activities during the prior fiscal year," and separately identifies what must accompany it: "Form RRF-1 along with either: Copy of IRS Form 990, 990-EZ, or 990-PF as filed with the IRS except: Schedule B is not requested or required by the Registry." A separate statutory subdivision layers additional financial-disclosure obligations onto larger organizations: an entity that "receives or accrues in any fiscal year gross revenue of two million dollars ($2,000,000) or more, exclusive of grants from, and contracts for services with, governmental entities for which the governmental entity requires an accounting of the funds received," must, among other things, "[p]repare annual financial statements using generally accepted accounting principles that are audited by an independent certified public accountant in conformity with generally accepted auditing standards." The same statute ties public disclosure of those audited statements to existing federal practice: "A charity shall make its annual audited financial statements available to the public in the same manner that is prescribed for IRS Form 990 by the latest revision of Section 6104(d) of the Internal Revenue Code and associated regulations."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]

  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12586(a), Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, the periodic written report requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12586.)
  "The first periodic written report, unless the filing thereof is suspended as herein provided, shall be filed not later than four months and 15 days following the close of the first calendar or fiscal year in which property is initially received."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12586(d), Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, the deadline for the first periodic report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12586.)
  "Every charitable corporation, unincorporated association, and trustee required to file reports with the Attorney General pursuant to this section that receives or accrues in any fiscal year gross revenue of two million dollars ($2,000,000) or more, exclusive of grants from, and contracts for services with, governmental entities for which the governmental entity requires an accounting of the funds received, shall do the following: (1) Prepare annual financial statements using generally accepted accounting principles that are audited by an independent certified public accountant in conformity with generally accepted auditing standards."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12586(e), Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, the $2,000,000 gross-revenue threshold requiring audited financial statements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12586.)
  "A charity shall make its annual audited financial statements available to the public in the same manner that is prescribed for IRS Form 990 by the latest revision of Section 6104(d) of the Internal Revenue Code and associated regulations."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12586(e), Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, tying public disclosure of audited financial statements to the IRS Form 990 disclosure practice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12586.)
  "The Form RRF-1 is a form to renew an existing registration to report on the charity's activities during the prior fiscal year."
  — California Attorney General, Registry of Charities and Fundraisers, “Initial Registration” page (state agency guidance page), California DOJ, Office of the Attorney General, Charities — Initial Registration, describing Form RRF-1 (https://oag.ca.gov/charities/initial-reg)
  "Form RRF-1 along with either: Copy of IRS Form 990, 990-EZ, or 990-PF as filed with the IRS except: Schedule B is not requested or required by the Registry."
  — California Attorney General, Registry of Charities and Fundraisers, “Renewals” page (state agency guidance page), California DOJ, Office of the Attorney General, Charities — Renewals, required annual filings (https://oag.ca.gov/charities/renewals)
  Known gap: The four Government Code quotations in this clause are drawn from subdivisions (a), (d), and (e) of the same statutory section, Cal. Gov. Code § 12586, and are treated as one statutory source describing different parts of a single reporting scheme, not as independent corroborating sources; the two Attorney General Registry webpage quotations (from the Registry's initial-registration and renewals pages) are cited separately as non-statutory sources for the specific form name and its accompanying documents, which the statutory text itself does not name, and this document independently fetched and verified the wording of both pages (each retrieved twice with different User-Agent strings, byte-identical after whitespace normalization). This clause does not cover the smaller-organization alternative to IRS Form 990 that the Registry's renewals page also references (a form the Registry calls Form CT-TR-1, not independently quoted here), the $2,000,000 revenue threshold's audit-committee composition requirements, or the officer-compensation-review requirement that the same statutory section separately imposes — none of which this clause's citations quote or this clause describes. It also does not cover the exception in § 12586(a) for certain corporate trustees regulated by state or federal banking authorities.

ATTORNEY GENERAL ENFORCEMENT AND STATUTORY PENALTIES
Failure to comply with the Registry's filing and reporting requirements exposes a covered entity, and in some circumstances a person acting for it, to statutory enforcement mechanisms distinct from any private lawsuit. The statute gives the Attorney General general authority to sue for compliance: "The Attorney General may institute appropriate proceedings to secure compliance with this article and to invoke the jurisdiction of the court." A separate statute creates a specific civil penalty for intentional violations: "Any person who violates any provision of this article with intent to deceive or defraud any charity or individual is liable for a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000)." That same statute also authorizes a distinct, accruing penalty not limited to intentional conduct: "The Attorney General may impose a penalty on any person or entity, not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) per act or omission, for each act or omission that constitutes a violation of this article or Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 300) of Division 1 of Title 11 of the California Code of Regulations," and, following required notice, "Penalties shall accrue, commencing on the fifth day after notice is given, at a rate of one hundred dollars ($100) per day for each day until that person or entity corrects that violation." Separately from these penalties, the statute also authorizes an additional monthly late fee when a covered entity does any of several listed things, including if it "(a) Exists and operates in California without being registered [or] (b) Solicits contributions in California without being registered or, if applicable, bonded."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The Attorney General may institute appropriate proceedings to secure compliance with this article and to invoke the jurisdiction of the court."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12591, Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, the Attorney General's general authority to sue for compliance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12591.)
  "Any person who violates any provision of this article with intent to deceive or defraud any charity or individual is liable for a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000)."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12591.1(a), Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, civil penalty for violations committed with intent to deceive or defraud (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12591.1.)
  "The Attorney General may impose a penalty on any person or entity, not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) per act or omission, for each act or omission that constitutes a violation of this article or Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 300) of Division 1 of Title 11 of the California Code of Regulations."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12591.1(c), Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, per-act-or-omission penalty authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12591.1.)
  "Penalties shall accrue, commencing on the fifth day after notice is given, at a rate of one hundred dollars ($100) per day for each day until that person or entity corrects that violation."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12591.1(c), Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, the daily accrual rate for uncorrected violations after notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12591.1.)
  "(a) Exists and operates in California without being registered. (b) Solicits contributions in California without being registered or, if applicable, bonded."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12586.1, Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, monthly late fee for operating or soliciting while unregistered (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12586.1.)
  Known gap: Cal. Gov. Code § 12591 is one independently enacted section; the two quotations drawn from Cal. Gov. Code § 12591.1 are both from subsection (c) of that section (except the civil-penalty quotation, which is subsection (a)) and, together with the subsection (a) quotation, are treated as one statutory source — non-adjacent parts of the same section — not as independent corroborating sources; Cal. Gov. Code § 12586.1 is a fourth, independently enacted section. This clause does not cover every remedy available to the Attorney General under § 12591.1 — that section separately authorizes cease-and-desist orders, suspension of registration, a hearing-and-review procedure, and injunctive relief including a receiver, restitution, or accounting, none of which are quoted here, though registration suspension is addressed from a different angle in this document's delinquency clause. It also does not evaluate whether any specific conduct would meet the "intent to deceive or defraud" standard for the $10,000 civil penalty, or whether any specific conduct falls within § 12586.1's list of late-fee triggers beyond the two quoted here — both are factual determinations this clause does not make.

DELINQUENCY, LOSS OF GOOD STANDING, AND RELATED CONSEQUENCES
Beyond the civil penalties a statute authorizes directly, the Attorney General's Registry also tracks each registrant's compliance status, and that status carries its own consequences once an entity falls behind on required filings. The Registry's own guidance describes the practical effect of delinquency in these terms: "A charitable organization that is not in good standing with the Registry because of delinquency, suspension, or revocation may not operate or solicit donations in California," a rule the Registry's guidance attributes to a specific California regulation, Cal. Code Regs., tit. 11, section 312. The Registry's guidance on the annual renewal filing separately describes a range of consequences that can follow from failing to renew registration on time: "The failure to renew registration may result in late fees, penalties, a delinquent registration status, suspended registration status, revoked registration status, or other legal action, and the loss of tax-exempt status with the California Franchise Tax Board."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A charitable organization that is not in good standing with the Registry because of delinquency, suspension, or revocation may not operate or solicit donations in California."
  — California Attorney General, Registry of Charities and Fundraisers, “Delinquency” page (state agency guidance page), California DOJ, Office of the Attorney General, Charities — Delinquency, effect of not being in good standing (https://oag.ca.gov/charities/delinquency)
  "The failure to renew registration may result in late fees, penalties, a delinquent registration status, suspended registration status, revoked registration status, or other legal action, and the loss of tax-exempt status with the California Franchise Tax Board."
  — California Attorney General, Registry of Charities and Fundraisers, “Renewals” page (state agency guidance page), California DOJ, Office of the Attorney General, Charities — Renewals, consequences of failing to renew registration (https://oag.ca.gov/charities/renewals)
  Known gap: Both quotations in this clause are drawn from Attorney General Registry of Charities and Fundraisers webpages (the Registry's Delinquency page and its Renewals page), not from the Government Code text itself, and are treated as two independent administrative sources describing the Registry's own compliance practices; this document independently fetched and verified the wording of these two webpages (each retrieved twice, with different User-Agent strings, and found byte-identical after whitespace normalization), but it did not independently fetch or verify the text of the regulation the Delinquency page cites, Cal. Code Regs., tit. 11, section 312 — that regulation's own wording is not quoted here, and only the Registry's own description of its effect is, consistent with this document's discipline of omitting rather than fabricating a quotation from a source it did not itself retrieve. Separately, the specific mechanics and legal basis of the loss of California Franchise Tax Board tax-exempt status mentioned on the Renewals page are governed by California Revenue and Taxation Code provisions this document does not cite or independently verify here. This clause does not state that any specific organization is delinquent, suspended, revoked, or has lost tax-exempt status; it describes only the consequences the Registry's own published guidance associates with those statuses generally.

expectedJSON.body: Once registered, a charitable corporation, unincorporated association, or trustee subject to the Registry is subject to a recurring, not merely one-time, reporting duty. The statute requires that, with certain exceptions, "every charitable corporation, unincorporated association, and trustee subject to this article shall, in addition to filing copies of the instruments previously required, file with the Attorney General periodic written reports, under oath, setting forth information as to the nature of the assets held for charitable purposes and the administration thereof by the corporation, unincorporated association, or trustee, in accordance with rules and regulations of the Attorney General." The statute itself fixes the deadline for the first such report: "The first periodic written report, unless the filing thereof is suspended as herein provided, shall be filed not later than four months and 15 days following the close of the first calendar or fiscal year in which property is initially received" — the same four-months-and-15-days period that governs each subsequent annual report. The Attorney General's Registry implements this statutory duty through a specific numbered form: its own guidance states that "the Form RRF-1 is a form to renew an existing registration to report on the charity's activities during the prior fiscal year," and separately identifies what must accompany it: "Form RRF-1 along with either: Copy of IRS Form 990, 990-EZ, or 990-PF as filed with the IRS except: Schedule B is not requested or required by the Registry." A separate statutory subdivision layers additional financial-disclosure obligations onto larger organizations: an entity that "receives or accrues in any fiscal year gross revenue of two million dollars ($2,000,000) or more, exclusive of grants from, and contracts for services with, governmental entities for which the governmental entity requires an accounting of the funds received," must, among other things, "[p]repare annual financial statements using generally accepted accounting principles that are audited by an independent certified public accountant in conformity with generally accepted auditing standards." The same statute ties public disclosure of those audited statements to existing federal practice: "A charity shall make its annual audited financial statements available to the public in the same manner that is prescribed for IRS Form 990 by the latest revision of Section 6104(d) of the Internal Revenue Code and associated regulations."

expectedJSON.body: Failure to comply with the Registry's filing and reporting requirements exposes a covered entity, and in some circumstances a person acting for it, to statutory enforcement mechanisms distinct from any private lawsuit. The statute gives the Attorney General general authority to sue for compliance: "The Attorney General may institute appropriate proceedings to secure compliance with this article and to invoke the jurisdiction of the court." A separate statute creates a specific civil penalty for intentional violations: "Any person who violates any provision of this article with intent to deceive or defraud any charity or individual is liable for a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000)." That same statute also authorizes a distinct, accruing penalty not limited to intentional conduct: "The Attorney General may impose a penalty on any person or entity, not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) per act or omission, for each act or omission that constitutes a violation of this article or Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 300) of Division 1 of Title 11 of the California Code of Regulations," and, following required notice, "Penalties shall accrue, commencing on the fifth day after notice is given, at a rate of one hundred dollars ($100) per day for each day until that person or entity corrects that violation." Separately from these penalties, the statute also authorizes an additional monthly late fee when a covered entity does any of several listed things, including if it "(a) Exists and operates in California without being registered [or] (b) Solicits contributions in California without being registered or, if applicable, bonded."

expectedJSON.body: Beyond the civil penalties a statute authorizes directly, the Attorney General's Registry also tracks each registrant's compliance status, and that status carries its own consequences once an entity falls behind on required filings. The Registry's own guidance describes the practical effect of delinquency in these terms: "A charitable organization that is not in good standing with the Registry because of delinquency, suspension, or revocation may not operate or solicit donations in California," a rule the Registry's guidance attributes to a specific California regulation, Cal. Code Regs., tit. 11, section 312. The Registry's guidance on the annual renewal filing separately describes a range of consequences that can follow from failing to renew registration on time: "The failure to renew registration may result in late fees, penalties, a delinquent registration status, suspended registration status, revoked registration status, or other legal action, and the loss of tax-exempt status with the California Franchise Tax Board."
